title: When the Phone Rings at 2 a.m.
subtitle: On the suicide, the accident, the diagnosis, and showing up to the worst day of someone's life without falling apart in it

sections.title: The Phone in the Dark
sections.body:
The phone rings and it is not a wrong number. It is two in the morning, and a voice you know is breaking apart on the other end, and a sentence is coming that will divide this family's life into before and after. You are awake now whether you want to be or not.

This is the work no seminary prepared you for, and it will come, and it will come more than once.

There is no script for the car ride to the hospital, the knock on the door at three a.m., the room where a mother has just been told her son is gone. You will arrive afraid and underqualified and that is the correct way to arrive. The temptation is to have words ready, to bring an explanation, to fill the unbearable silence with something theological. Resist it. The first thing you bring is not an answer. It is your body, your face, your willingness to be in the room when everyone wishes there were no such room. I have stood in those rooms with nothing prepared and learned that nothing prepared was sometimes exactly right.

sections.title: Show Up and Stay
sections.body:
Go. That is the first commandment of crisis care and almost the whole of it. Get dressed and go, even when you do not know what you will do when you arrive.

Do not say I am praying for you and roll over. Say I am on my way. Then be on your way.

Your presence is doing something your words cannot. It is telling a person in freefall that they have not been abandoned, that the floor of the universe has not entirely given out, that God has at least sent someone. When you get there, do not perform. Hold the coffee. Make the phone calls they cannot make. Stand in the hallway and intercept the relatives so the closest grievers can have a moment to breathe. Sit with them in the silence and do not rush to break it. The ministry of the early hours is mostly logistics and presence, the unglamorous serving that frees a shattered family to fall apart safely. You are the steady thing in the room. That does not mean you feel steady. It means you have decided to be the one who does not run.

sections.title: The Things You Must Not Say
sections.body:
In the worst hour, the wrong sentence does damage that lasts for decades, and most of the wrong sentences are reached for precisely because the silence is unbearable to you, not to them.

Guard your mouth. The grieving will remember what you said in that room for the rest of their lives.

Do not say everything happens for a reason. Do not say God needed them more than you did. Do not say at least, which is the deadliest phrase in the language of grief, because there is no at least at the foot of a tragedy and the person who says it has just told the sufferer their pain is being measured and found small. Do not explain. Do not defend God, who does not need your defense and has not asked for it. Do not, above all, say you understand, because you do not, and even if you have suffered the same thing your suffering was yours and not theirs. What you can say is small and true. I am so sorry. I am here. You do not have to talk. I am not going anywhere. And often the most pastoral thing you will do is say nothing at all and simply weep with those who weep, which Scripture commands and which most of us are too anxious to obey.

sections.title: When It Is a Suicide
sections.body:
There is a particular call that lands differently, and you must think about it before it comes, because it will come and you will not be able to think clearly once it does. A family has lost someone to suicide.

This grief is wrapped in a horror the others are not. It carries shame, blame, and a theological terror the family may be too frightened to speak.

They are asking, somewhere underneath, whether the person they loved is damned. Old and cruel teaching has told them so. Do not feed that. Do not stand in that house and pronounce on the eternal state of a soul, in either direction, because you do not know and God has not made you the judge. What you can say is that their loved one died of an illness as real as cancer, an illness of the mind that lied to them and stole their ability to see any way out. You can say that the God who searches hearts knew the full weight of what their loved one was carrying. You can refuse the blame the survivors are heaping on themselves, the endless if only, because that blame will eat them alive and it is not the truth. And you must do one more thing. You must watch the survivors, because suicide in a family raises the risk to everyone left, and you must make sure the living get to the help they need. Get the crisis number into their hands. Stay close in the months after, when the casseroles stop and the questions begin. This is not the funeral where you can lean on easy hope. This is the funeral where you stand in the dark and hold a candle and refuse to lie about either the darkness or the candle.

sections.title: Without Falling Apart in It
sections.body:
You absorb these nights into your body, and they do not leave when the family thanks you and you drive home in the dark. They accumulate. No one warns you how much of this a pastor carries.

You cannot keep showing up to the worst day of other people's lives if you never tend the toll it takes on yours.

So build the things that let you keep going. Have someone you can call after, a fellow pastor or a counselor, someone who can receive what you cannot carry alone. Do not be the steady one in every room and the broken one in none. That is a lie, and it ends in collapse or in a hardness that makes you useless to the very people you are trying to serve. Take the next day slow when you can. Let yourself grieve the things you witnessed, because if you stop feeling them you have not gotten stronger, you have gone numb, and a numb shepherd cannot weep with those who weep. The crucified Lord sweat blood in a garden the night before the worst day of his life. If he did not face the dark unmoved, you do not have to either. Go to the crisis. Stay in it. Then go and be held yourself, so that next time the phone rings, there is still a whole person to answer it.
